description: We’re a team of students from Pakistan, who believe space data should solve problems on the ground. We bring together product thinking, physics, competitive programming, and full-stack development, and we’re here to turn NASA’s open data into a tool that’s simple, practical, and genuinely useful to real people. Our goal is to build something that works, not just something that looks good in a demo.
summary: We built HindSight, a free web app that replays a farmer’s crop rotation through 40 real years of NASA weather before they commit a season to it. Rotation advice usually rests on long-term averages, and averages hide the bad years. HindSight takes NASA POWER daily weather (1984–2024) for any field on Earth. It runs the farmer’s current rotation and up to five alternatives through every day with an FAO-56 soil-water model. It shows how often each option would have failed, how much water it needs and how it did in the worst years. It explains why in plain language, next to a list of what the model doesn’t know. At Chakwal, Pakistan, the usual wheat-then-fallow rotation failed in 14 of 40 seasons. Field pea then fallow failed in 8, with half the water demand. Without being told, the engine picked out the 2012 US drought and Pakistan’s 1998–2002 drought, and its scores track NASA MODIS crop greenness. Farms are not broken by their average year, so they need to plan for the weather they actually get.
details:
HindSight replays a farmer’s crop rotation through 40 real years of NASA weather before they risk a season on it.

Farmers in places like Chakwal, Pakistan, pick a rotation once and live with it for years. The advice they get is usually built on long-term averages, and averages hide the bad years. At Chakwal, the common wheat-then-fallow rotation looks safe on average. But when we ran it day by day through NASA POWER weather from 1985 to 2024, it fell below our failure line in 14 of 40 seasons. That includes five years in a row, from 1998 to 2002.

How it works. You choose your field on a map or from a preset. You enter your soil and water situation, build the rotation you grow now, and set your priorities with sliders: steady harvests in bad years, water use, fodder, nitrogen, erosion, soil organic matter and market. HindSight downloads 41 years of daily NASA POWER weather for that point: rain, temperature, humidity, wind and sunshine. It then runs your rotation and up to five alternatives through every one of those days.

The model is a daily soil-water balance for the crop’s root zone, from FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper 56. Crop response to water stress comes from FAO-33, temperature limits from FAO EcoCrop, and the effect of a legume on the next crop from a published study. Soil water carries over from one crop to the next, so the order of crops matters. One question means about 344,000 simulated field-days, and the server answers in under a second.

What you see.

  • A “barcode” puts each rotation in a row and each year in a cell, so drought years show up as dark columns.
  • Cards show how often each option failed, its water demand, and how it did in your five worst years.
  • A Robust badge appears when the top pick keeps its place after we re-run everything with NASA rainfall 30% lower and 30% higher.
  • A climate-shift table compares 1985–2004 with 2005–2024.
  • Every result has a plain-language explanation, a list of what we don’t know, and points to check with a local expert. These sentences are filled in from the computed numbers. No AI model writes the advice.

Does it match reality? The engine is never told when droughts happened, yet it finds them:

  • Its worst years at Ames, Iowa include 2012 and 1988, which match the 2012 US Corn Belt drought.
  • Its worst years at Chakwal are 2001, 1998, 2000 and 2002, which match Pakistan’s 1998–2002 drought.
  • At Chakwal, our yearly scores also track NASA MODIS crop greenness from orbit (r = 0.59 over 24 years, p = 0.003).

Example result. At Chakwal, field pea then fallow would have failed in 8 of 40 seasons instead of 14. It needs about half the water (179 mm a year against 359 mm), and it held up better in the five worst years. It stays ranked first under every stress test we ran.

Benefits and impact. Farmers and extension workers can test a change before betting a season on it, using the real range of weather their field has seen. It works for any point on Earth, with no sensors, accounts or fees. Every number is labelled as a NASA estimate, a published value, a farmer input or a simulation result. It supports local knowledge rather than replacing it. The work connects to UN goals 2 (Zero Hunger), 6 (Clean Water), 13 (Climate Action) and 15 (Life on Land).

What makes it creative. Most tools ask what the average year looks like. We ask how your plan would have done in every year your field actually lived through. We show the answer as one picture a farmer can read at a glance.

What we considered.

  • NASA POWER weather is a grid-cell estimate about 50 km wide, not a field measurement. At Chakwal its rainfall runs about 48% above WorldClim, which is why every ranking is stress-tested on rainfall.
  • The index covers water and temperature only. Pests, disease, nutrients and crop varieties are not modelled.
  • Crop values are generic FAO figures. We left out crops such as rice because we could not find a published value for how sensitive they are to water stress.
  • The past 40 years are not a forecast.
  • We kept the interface simple enough for an extension worker to use with a farmer, and we show each limit next to the result it affects.

Next steps. Field trials with farmers and extension workers in Chakwal, more crops with sourced values, NASA SMAP soil moisture, and an Urdu interface with SMS summaries.

Tools. Python 3.11 with NumPy, SciPy, pandas, FastAPI, Uvicorn, Pydantic and pytest for the engine and API. TypeScript with React 18, Vite, Tailwind CSS, and Leaflet with OpenStreetMap for the web app. Docker for deployment, GitHub for code. No special hardware: it runs on a small cloud server and works in any browser.

MODIS/Terra Vegetation Indices 16-Day L3 Global 250m (MOD13Q1 v061)
ORNL DAAC MODIS and VIIRS Land Products Global Subsetting and Visualization Tool
MERRA-2 (the reanalysis behind POWER’s weather data)
CERES (the solar radiation behind POWER’s data)
projectRefs: FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper 56 (Allen et al. 1998)
FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper 66 (Steduto et al. 2012), yield-response factors
Saxton and Rawls 2006, soil water from texture
Zhao et al. 2022, legume effect on the next crop
Bowles et al. 2020, rotation diversity and drought
WorldClim 2.1 climate normals for Chakwal (via Population Review)
NOAA climate normals for Ames, Iowa (via Climate-Zone)
Claude by Anthropic (coding, research and writing assistant)
